title: Ann McGinty and Kentucky's first spinning wheel
summary: Ann McGinty brought the first spinning wheel over Cumberland Gap in 1775 and helped make linsey-woolsey cloth at Harrodstown, a frontier staple.
bodyMarkdown:
Ann McGinty came to Kentucky with the tools of a household economy. Born Anne Kennedy around 1735 in Virginia, she arrived in September 1775 with her husband William Poage (also spelled Pogue) and their children, first at Boonesborough and then at [Fort Harrod](https://grokipedia.com/page/old_fort_harrod_state_park). Like other families, they came by the trace through [Cumberland Gap](https://grokipedia.com/page/Cumberland_Gap).

Her cargo is what made her famous. Accounts credit her with bringing the first spinning wheel to Kentucky, carried on horseback over the mountains. The [Kentucky Historical Society's ExploreKYHistory](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/983) entry describes the household equipment as a loom, and other accounts describe a spinning wheel. A University of Kentucky history reconciles the two accounts: she came with her "precious spinning wheel tied to her horse and plans for a loom folded in her pocket."

At Fort Harrod, according to the [University of Kentucky's history of pioneer women](https://publications.mgcafe.uky.edu/sites/publications.ca.uky.edu/files/fcs1323.pdf), she tried local weeds and grasses and spun thread from nettle until flax could be grown, dyeing the dull cloth with bark, berries and nuts. She is credited with spinning [linsey-woolsey](https://grokipedia.com/page/Linsey-woolsey), a sturdy fabric woven from linen and wool once settlers had flax and sheep. She taught other women at the fort to spin, weave and sew, and her husband William Poage made looms for neighbors.

Her life was marked by the violence and loss of the frontier. She married four times and outlived several husbands; genealogical sources say William Poage was killed in 1778 and a later husband died at the [Battle of Blue Licks](https://grokipedia.com/page/Battle_of_Blue_Licks) in 1782, though those details rest on family records rather than documentary sources. She bore eight children, two of whom died in infancy.

McGinty also prospered in ways that reflect her time. She ran a mill and was licensed to keep an ordinary, or tavern, in 1786–87, and her household relied on the labor of enslaved people. That reliance was common among Kentucky's early landholding families and is part of the full story of the community she helped build.

## Kentucky today

McGinty died in 1815 and is buried in the Pioneer Graveyard at [Harrodsburg](https://grokipedia.com/page/Harrodsburg,_Kentucky), where a [marker](https://www.hmdb.org/m.asp?m=46523) credits her with Kentucky's first spinning wheel. [Old Fort Harrod State Park](https://grokipedia.com/page/old_fort_harrod_state_park) includes a reconstruction of the fort and what the park calls the oldest cemetery west of the Alleghenies, which keeps the frontier community she helped clothe on view.
